findings.issue_text: [BUG] The new code references `organization_context.member.has_global_access`, but `organization_context` is neither defined in `get()` nor imported/added anywhere in this diff, so every GET on this endpoint raises NameError. The expression is evaluated unconditionally on every request (before the `use_optimized` check), so the audit-log listing endpoint returns a 500 for all users — admins, regular members, and callers that never send `optimized_pagination` — breaking the endpoint entirely.

[BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator subclasses BasePaginator but its `get_result` calls `self.build_queryset(...)` and `get_item_key` reads `self.key` and it passes `is_desc=self.desc`, none of which exist on BasePaginator (they are defined on CursorPaginator), and it is constructed with an `order_by` kwarg that BasePaginator does not accept. The first request routed through this paginator crashes: either `TypeError: __init__() got an unexpected keyword argument 'order_by'` at construction in `self.paginate(...)`, or, if construction succeeds, `AttributeError: 'OptimizedCursorPaginator' object has no attribute 'build_queryset'` — the class is unusable as written.

[BUG] The negative-offset branch relies on the comment's claim that 'the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically', but Django raises `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported.` for a queryset slice with a negative start, so `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with `start_offset < 0` crashes. An admin who sends a cursor with a negative offset (Cursor.__init__ does `int(offset)` and accepts it) hits an unhandled AssertionError surfaced as a 500, instead of the 'efficient bidirectional pagination' the feature advertises.

[ADVISORY] The same false assumption is baked into the modified base paginator: `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` deliberately passes through negative offsets for prev cursors where Django's slice will raise AssertionError. The inconsistency between the clamped non-prev path and the unclamped prev path means any prev cursor carrying a negative offset 500s; the next maintainer extending this code inherits two silently different offset semantics in adjacent lines.

[ADVISORY] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result is a near-verbatim copy-paste of CursorPaginator.get_result instead of subclassing CursorPaginator, and the copy has already drifted (the base version got the `max(0, offset)` clamp while this copy reuses raw `offset` in the prev-branch `len(results) == offset + limit + extra` comparison). Any future fix to cursor handling must now be applied in two places; the drift already present means the two paginators behave differently for prev cursors, and a fix landed in one will silently not apply to the other.

[ADVISORY] process_batch now unconditionally reads `val["end_timestamp_precise"]` with no fallback, so messages produced by pre-deploy producers that lack this field crash the consumer with KeyError. During a rolling deploy, retained messages on the ingest-spans topic produced by old code are consumed by the new consumer and raise KeyError inside process_batch, stalling the spans processing consumer on those offsets until manual intervention.

[ADVISORY] New behavior is gated on the raw query parameter `optimized_pagination` with no feature flag or options entry, so it cannot be disabled without a code deploy. If the optimized path misbehaves in production, operators have no kill switch short of rolling back the release, and the undocumented parameter becomes part of the de-facto public API surface.

[ADVISORY] The diff adds ~95 lines of new non-trivial pagination logic (OptimizedCursorPaginator, including the negative-offset branch) with no tests anywhere in the diff. The new paginator's first execution in production is also its first execution ever; any of the construction/attribute failures above, or cursor-handling regressions, would reach users with zero test coverage to catch them.

[BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator extends BasePaginator but never implements build_queryset, which BasePaginator only provides as a NotImplementedError stub, so get_result raises NotImplementedError the first time the optimized audit-log path executes. A superuser or global-access member requesting /organizations/{org}/audit-logs/?optimized_pagination=true gets a 500 (NotImplementedError) instead of paginated audit rows; the new pagination feature is dead on arrival because no test exercises the endpoint's optimized branch.

[BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key calls math.floor(value)/math.ceil(value) directly on getattr(item, self.key) with no datetime-to-epoch conversion, while the audit endpoint invokes it with order_by="-datetime" where item values are datetime objects. math.floor(datetime.datetime) raises TypeError, so even after build_queryset is fixed the optimized audit-log page crashes with a 500 when build_cursor invokes get_item_key on the first result; the datetime coercion that CursorPaginator.get_item_key performs was silently dropped in the copy.

[BUG] The 'advanced' negative-offset branch executes queryset[start_offset:stop] with a negative start, but Django QuerySet slicing raises AssertionError ('Negative indexing is not allowed') for negative start indices — the comment's claim that the ORM handles negative slicing is false. An authorized admin who submits any cursor with a negative offset (a cursor value is client-controlled input parsed in src/sentry/utils/cursors.py) gets a 500 AssertionError from the optimized audit-log endpoint; the headline 'negative offset support' feature cannot work against a Django queryset as written.

[BUG] zunionstore is called without AGGREGATE, so Redis's default SUM aggregates scores when a payload exists in both set_key and span_key (or parent_key), doubling the end_timestamp_precise score instead of keeping the original timestamp as the old sunionstore set semantics did. Merged duplicate spans get a score roughly double their real timestamp (~year 2039+), so the zpopmin eviction at line 62 evicts the wrong spans (recent duplicated spans are treated as oldest and dropped first), corrupting eviction order for traces where child and parent buffers overlap.

[BUG] process_batch reads val["end_timestamp_precise"] unconditionally, so any ingest_spans_v1 message produced without that field crashes the consumer with KeyError instead of being handled with a default. Messages already in the topic from producers that have not yet deployed the new field (or any producer path that omits it) raise KeyError in process_batch, stalling the partition on a poison message during the rolling deploy window until offsets are manually skipped.

[ADVISORY] The max_segment_spans guard (metric + segment skip on span-count overflow) was deleted, leaving the count bound solely to a hardcoded 1000 inside add-buffer.lua's eviction, which only runs on the Lua merge path — the direct p.zadd insertion path in process_spans (lines 197-198) has no eviction in this diff. Segments populated via the Python zadd path can exceed any span-count bound because the only in-diff eviction lives in the Lua script; operators lose both the previous overflow metric and the configurable limit, and the limit 1000 is now duplicated as a magic number on the Redis side with no single source of truth against the old max_segment_spans setting.

[ADVISORY] The zpopmin eviction silently deletes the oldest spans from the set with no metric, log, or error signal, replacing the previous overflow behavior which emitted spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_size_exceeded / segment_span_count_exceeded metrics and an error log. When a trace exceeds 1000 buffered spans, spans are permanently dropped from the buffer with zero observability — on-call cannot distinguish eviction-driven data loss from absence of traffic, and there is no way to measure eviction rate in production.

[ADVISORY] The redirect-resolution loop limit was cut from 10000 to 1000 and the comment documenting the consequence (segment trees deeper than the limit are not joined correctly) was deleted, with no accompanying test for deep redirect chains. Traces whose parent-redirect chains exceed depth 1000 will now silently resolve to the wrong set key, mis-parenting spans; the removed comment was the only documentation of this known failure mode, and the behavioral motivation for changing 10000 to 1000 is unrecorded and untested.

[ADVISORY] The new OptimizedCursorPaginator class and the audit endpoint's optimized branch have zero test coverage — the only test files touched in this diff are under tests/sentry/spans/, and none exercise paginator.py or src/sentry/api/endpoints/organization_auditlogs.py. A regression in the new paginator (e.g., the build_queryset/get_item_key defects above) ships undetected; the negative-offset feature, the admin gating, and the fallback-to-DateTimePaginator branch all lack the assertions that would catch the 500s this class currently produces.

[ADVISORY] The scard→zcard, sunionstore→zunionstore conversion and the new eviction branch in add-buffer.lua have no test coverage in this diff — tests/sentry/spans/test_buffer.py was only touched to add end_timestamp_precise fields and exercises the Python path, not the Lua merge/evict logic. A regression in the merge (e.g., the SUM-aggregate score corruption) or eviction (dropping the wrong spans) reaches production unverified; the eviction and count-pop behavior — the actual point of this change — is the only new spans logic with no assertion anywhere.

[ADVISORY] OptimizedCursorPaginator subclasses BasePaginator and hand-copies ~50 lines of CursorPaginator.get_result (cursor handling, hits counting, prev-trim, build_cursor call) instead of subclassing CursorPaginator, and the copy has already drifted: the base class clamps negative offsets while the copy conditionally allows them. The next fix to cursor slicing or hits accounting must be applied in two places (BasePaginator.get_result and this copy) and drift like the existing datetime-handling omission goes unnoticed; subclassing CursorPaginator would delete the duplicated block and inherit its correct datetime key handling.

[ADVISORY] The optimized pagination behavior is gated on a raw query parameter (optimized_pagination == "true") plus inline code-level admin checks, with no feature flag or options entry controlling it. If the optimized path misbehaves in production (which the defects above make likely), it cannot be disabled without a code deploy — any admin can activate it per-request and there is no kill switch, violating the rollout-safety pattern used for other endpoint behavior changes.

[ADVISORY] end_timestamp_precise was added to the Span NamedTuple as a required positional field (before the defaulted is_segment_span), but the diff only updates the two constructor sites it happens to include (factory.py and the span tests); no verification that every Span( construction site in the codebase was updated. Any out-of-diff Span( construction site (other consumers, replay/tooling code) that omits the new field raises TypeError at runtime, and positional-argument call sites silently shift is_segment_span into end_timestamp_precise, corrupting the zadd score to a boolean.

[BUG] The audit-logs endpoint gains an entirely new admin-gated 'optimized pagination' API mode selected by an undocumented raw query parameter (optimized_pagination=true), which is unrelated work smuggled into a PR titled 'Optimize spans buffer insertion with eviction during insert' and traceable to no requirement in the spans buffer work. Reviewers and operators cannot evaluate this behavior change against the stated intent; the new code path (new paginator, new authorization branch, new client-controlled mode switch with no feature flag or options entry so it cannot be disabled without a code deploy) ships silently inside an infrastructural PR, and any regression in it surfaces as audit-log breakage with no rollback lever.

[BUG] The diff modifies the shared CursorPaginator.get_result slicing logic (start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset), changing behavior for every endpoint in the codebase that uses CursorPaginator, which is untraceable to the spans-buffer eviction requirement. Non-prev cursors with negative offsets (which clients can supply by forging a cursor string) previously raised Django's AssertionError on negative slicing and now silently clamp to 0, returning page-1 data for a malformed cursor on every paginated endpoint — a silent API-surface behavior change riding in a spans PR with no changelog or requirement backing it.

[BUG] The OptimizedCursorPaginator negative-offset branch executes queryset[start_offset:stop] with a negative start_offset, which raises Django's AssertionError ('Negative indexing is not supported'), directly contradicting the adjacent comment claiming 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically'. Any request to the audit-logs endpoint with optimized_pagination=true and a client-supplied cursor carrying a negative offset (the exact input this 'advanced feature' branch exists to handle) crashes with a 500 instead of returning paginated results; the feature's sole distinguishing code path is non-functional.

[ADVISORY] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result is a ~90-line copy of CursorPaginator.get_result differing only in the negative-offset branch and an added enable_advanced_features flag, creating a second hand-maintained copy of core pagination logic. The next fix to cursor-pagination boundary handling (the extra/is_prev logic, build_cursor interplay, hit counting) must be applied in two places or the two paginators silently diverge — exactly the class of drift this copy already exhibits (the base version clamps offsets, the copy conditionally does not).

[ADVISORY] The enable_advanced_features flag and negative-offset support have no internal producer anywhere in the diff — negative offsets reach the paginator only via client-forged cursor query strings, so the 'advanced feature' is speculative generality whose only activation path is attacker-controlled input. The code ships a capability no requirement calls for, whose sole reachable trigger is a hand-crafted cursor parameter, meaning it is either dead weight or an undocumented client-facing behavior expansion; both outcomes fail the traceability bar.

[ADVISORY] No test in this diff exercises OptimizedCursorPaginator, the modified CursorPaginator slicing, or the audit-logs endpoint's new optimized_pagination branch — all new behavior-bearing logic ships untested. A regression in the new paginator (e.g., the negative-slicing crash above or a boundary error in the copied prev-cursor trimming) would ship to the audit-logs endpoint undetected by CI.

[BUG] The redirect-resolution loop limit is silently cut from 10000 to 1000 and the comment documenting the known limitation ('segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly') is deleted — a behavioral invariant reduction untraceable to the eviction intent in the PR title. Segment trees deeper than 1000 that previously resolved their root set now terminate the loop early and attach spans to the wrong set, producing incorrectly joined traces; the guardrail comment that documented this tradeoff for future maintainers is removed at the same time, hiding the failure mode.

[ADVISORY] Eviction via zpopmin silently discards the oldest unflushed spans from the buffer with no metric or log, while the old code path this replaces emitted metrics.incr('spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_size_exceeded') and an error log whenever data was dropped. Operators lose spans for high-volume traces (data loss by design) with zero observability signal — the dropped-span rate, which determines whether the 1000 cap is misconfigured for a customer's trace size, is invisible until users report incomplete traces.

[ADVISORY] The Span NamedTuple gains a required end_timestamp_precise field with no default value, so every Span construction site outside this diff raises TypeError: missing required argument the moment this code deploys. Any producer of Span objects not updated in this PR (other ingestion paths, tooling, out-of-tree subclasses of SpansBuffer) crashes at construction time; the diff only updates the sites it happens to touch, and the required-without-default placement (before is_segment_span, which has a default) forecloses any call site that relied on positional is_segment_span.

[BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator subclasses BasePaginator instead of CursorPaginator, so its get_result calls self.build_queryset() and self.count_hits() (and build_cursor invokes self.get_item_key -> self._is_asc), none of which are defined on BasePaginator — they exist only on CursorPaginator — so the first request to the audit-log endpoint with optimized_pagination=true raises AttributeError and returns a 500. The entire advertised optimization path is dead code: any superuser or global-access member passing ?optimized_pagination=true gets a 500 instead of audit log results; additionally, even if the missing methods existed, get_item_key would raise TypeError because math.ceil/math.floor are called on the datetime value from order_by='-datetime', which the previous DateTimePaginator existed specifically to convert.

[BUG] The 'negative offset' advanced branch slices the Django queryset with a negative start index (queryset[cursor.offset:stop] with cursor.offset < 0), which Django's QuerySet.__getitem__ rejects with AssertionError('Negative indexing is not supported') — the inline comment claiming 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is false. Any admin who submits a cursor with a negative offset to the audit-log endpoint gets a 500 from an AssertionError instead of a 4xx; the feature the branch exists to provide is unimplementable as written because ORM slicing cannot represent negative offsets, so the whole negative-offset design needs to be discarded rather than fixed.

[BUG] process_batch reads val["end_timestamp_precise"] with a hard subscript, so any span message on the ingest-spans topic produced without that field (messages already in the topic from before the field was emitted, or producer paths where the field is optional) raises KeyError inside the consumer's processing strategy. A single message lacking the field becomes a repeating poison pill: the batch raises on every consumption attempt, stalling span ingestion for that partition until manual intervention, rather than degrading (e.g., defaulting the score or skipping the record with a metric).

[ADVISORY] The zpopmin eviction silently deletes the oldest spans (lowest end_timestamp_precise) from a segment set with no metric or log, replacing the previous overflow behavior which emitted the segment_span_count_exceeded metric and logged an error. When a live segment accumulates more than 1000 child spans, the evicted spans are removed from Redis before any flush and are never written to storage — silent, unobservable trace data loss on high-fanout traces; operators have no signal that eviction is occurring, where the old code path at least incremented a metric on every oversized segment.

[ADVISORY] The max_segment_spans span-count guard in _load_segment_data was deleted, so the only remaining bound on per-segment payload materialization is max_segment_bytes, and the new 1000-span zpopmin cap in add-buffer.lua applies only to the Lua merge path — the process_spans pipeline zadd path (lines 194-199) has no cap at all. A segment of many small spans written via process_spans grows without a count limit; the flusher then materializes up to max_segment_bytes of payloads per key in memory (where the deleted count guard previously stopped it earlier), and the max_segment_spans setting is now enforced nowhere — a silently retired safety limit.

[ADVISORY] Lowering the redirect-chain loop bound from 10000 to 1000 silently narrows the documented safety limit — the deleted comment stated that beyond the bound segment trees may not be joined correctly, and the new code drops that caveat without any metric or error when the bound is exhausted. Traces whose parent-redirect chains exceed depth 1000 now terminate the loop with set_span_id pointing at an intermediate node, so the span is attached to the wrong segment's set and data lands under the wrong parent — a correctness regression for deep trees that previously resolved, with no observability.

[ADVISORY] The new pagination behavior is gated on the raw query parameter optimized_pagination with no feature flag or option entry, and non-admins requesting it are silently switched back to the legacy paginator with no indication in the response. The behavior cannot be disabled or rolled back without a code deploy, and clients who send optimized_pagination=true but lack global access receive a silently different (unoptimized) response shape/behavior than the feature implies, making the gate undiagnosable from the client side.

[ADVISORY] OptimizedCursorPaginator duplicates CursorPaginator.get_result almost line-for-line (and patches the shared CursorPaginator.get_result at lines 178-184 to accommodate it) instead of subclassing CursorPaginator, and the copy has already drifted: the prev-branch trim check compares len(results) == offset + limit + extra using the raw offset even in the negative-offset branch where results were sliced from start_offset. Two parallel pagination implementations must now be maintained in lockstep; the next fix to cursor edge handling in CursorPaginator will not reach OptimizedCursorPaginator, and the trim check in the advanced branch compares against an arithmetic that no longer describes the slice actually taken.

[ADVISORY] The only test changes for the spans buffer thread the new end_timestamp_precise field through existing fixtures; no test in the diff exercises the zpopmin eviction path, the zscan pairing changes in _load_segment_data, or the deep-redirect bound reduction. A regression in the eviction arithmetic (e.g., popping the wrong end of the zset, or evicting when span_count is fetched before the current span is added) or in the zscan-to-payload mapping would pass the entire test suite while silently dropping or corrupting span data in production.

[ADVISORY] The PR's stated objective is 'Optimize spans buffer insertion with eviction during insert', but the diff silently bundles an entirely unrelated admin-gated pagination feature (audit logs endpoint branch, new OptimizedCursorPaginator class, Cursor offset changes) into the same change. Reviewers and approvers accepted a spans-buffer performance change, but unrelated API-surface code ships under that acceptance; the comments in this hunk ('This is safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level', 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically') are self-rationalizations of behavior no reviewer was asked to accept. This is exactly the objective-drift pattern where a later iteration redefines the deliverable without explicit human sign-off, and it hides the pagination bugs in this diff behind a performance-PR title.

[BUG] `organization_context` is not defined anywhere in this endpoint (the method signature receives `organization` and `member` directly), so `organization_context.member.has_global_access` raises NameError on every GET request. Every call to the organization audit-logs list endpoint — including the default, non-optimized path — raises NameError and returns a 500 instead of paginated audit results; the audit log API is completely broken for all users, not just the new admin path.

[BUG] The 'advanced feature' negative-offset branch slices the queryset with a negative start (`queryset[start_offset:stop]` where `start_offset = cursor.offset < 0`), but Django QuerySets raise `ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported.` for negative slice starts — the inline claim that 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is false. Any admin request to the audit-logs endpoint with `optimized_pagination=true` and a negative cursor offset raises ValueError mid-request and returns a 500; the headline feature of the new paginator cannot execute its distinguishing code path at all.

[BUG] The endpoint switches to OptimizedCursorPaginator with `order_by="-datetime"` but never passes a `key`, while DateTimePaginator (the previous class) sets `key="datetime"` in its own __init__ — so cursor boundary values are computed from the default pk attribute via `math.ceil(value)` while rows are ordered by datetime. Cursor continuation filters on pk values that contradict the -datetime sort order, so page boundaries are wrong: admins browsing audit logs with the optimized flag get skipped and duplicated entries across pages, silently corrupting audit review.

[BUG] The parent-chain redirect limit was silently reduced from 10000 to 1000 and the comment documenting the accepted tradeoff ('theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly') was deleted rather than re-justified. Trace trees whose parent-chain depth is between 1001 and 10000 — which previously resolved to the correct root and were joined correctly — now exhaust the loop and attach spans to a mid-chain ancestor set, producing incorrectly assembled segments; the original accepted constraint was changed with no explicit human acceptance or replacement mitigation.

[ADVISORY] The new eviction path (`zpopmin` when `span_count > 1000`) silently drops the oldest spans with no metric or log, replacing the previous oversized-segment handling that emitted `metrics.incr(...segment_span_count_exceeded)` and an error log before skipping. Span data loss (previously at least observable and alertable) becomes completely silent: when a segment set exceeds 1000 members the oldest spans are evicted before flush and no operator signal fires, so trace incompleteness is discovered only by users.

[ADVISORY] The `max_segment_spans` enforcement block was deleted, leaving that setting unenforced on the read side while the write side now uses a hardcoded 1000 cap inside the Lua script — two different, hand-maintained constants where one config used to be the single source of truth. Operators who tune `max_segment_spans` get no effect on actual behavior, and anyone reasoning about the eviction cap must know to look for a magic number buried in a Lua script; the next change to span-count limits gets harder and is likely to miss one of the two sites.

[ADVISORY] BasePaginator.get_result — the shared paginator used by every cursor-paginated endpoint in the codebase — was modified (negative non-prev offsets now clamp to 0 instead of raising ValueError from Django slicing) purely to accommodate the unrelated OptimizedCursorPaginator feature. All existing endpoints silently change behavior for malformed/negative cursor offsets (500 → silent first page) without any of their owners being asked; a shared-class contract was altered as a hidden dependency of the bundled pagination feature rather than as an accepted change.

[ADVISORY] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result is a ~70-line verbatim copy of BasePaginator.get_result with only the negative-offset branch added, and the copy has already drifted: the is_prev trim compares `len(results) == offset + limit + extra` using the raw offset while the slice above uses `start_offset`. Every future fix to BasePaginator pagination logic (boundary handling, is_prev trimming) must be manually replicated here or the two paginators diverge further; the duplicated trim condition is already inconsistent with the duplicated slice for negative offsets.

[ADVISORY] New admin-only pagination behavior is gated on a raw undocumented query parameter (`optimized_pagination == "true"`) with no feature flag or options entry. If the optimized path misbehaves in production (see the negative-offset and cursor-key defects above), it cannot be disabled without a code deploy; behavior is also silently discoverable by any admin who guesses the parameter, outside the normal feature-flag rollout process.

[ADVISORY] Replacing `sunionstore` with `zunionstore` changes duplicate-member semantics: zunionstore's default AGGREGATE is SUM, so a payload present in both `set_key` and `span_key`/`parent_key` gets its end_timestamp_precise score doubled instead of deduplicated as under sadd. Re-merged spans get inflated scores (e.g., ~2x epoch seconds, a timestamp far in the future), so the zpopmin eviction orders them as newest and never evicts them while correctly-scored spans get evicted around them — eviction targets the wrong members whenever the merged sets overlap.

[ADVISORY] The new OptimizedCursorPaginator class — including its enable_advanced_features branch, boundary handling, and is_prev trimming — has no test coverage anywhere in this diff, and the audit endpoint's new two-branch get() (which cannot currently even run to completion) is likewise untested. The negative-offset crash and the pk-vs-datetime cursor-key mismatch above would both pass CI today; any regression in this entirely new pagination state machine ships silently to the admin audit-log path.

[BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator is incompatible with the datetime ordering the audit endpoint uses: get_item_key calls math.floor/math.ceil on getattr(item, self.key) where self.key is 'datetime' (order_by='-datetime'), and build_queryset (line 856) filters the DateTimeField against the integer cursor value, so both raise (TypeError on floor(datetime) / ValidationError on datetime__lt 0) on the very first request. Every privileged user (superuser or has_global_access member) who requests /organizations/<slug>/audit-logs/?optimized_pagination=true gets an unhandled exception and a 500 instead of paginated audit logs; the new 'optimized' path can never return a successful response, and there is no metric or alert to reveal that the feature is dead on arrival.

[BUG] The 'advanced' negative-offset branch slices the Django queryset with a negative start (queryset[start_offset:stop] with start_offset = cursor.offset < 0), which Django QuerySet does not support — slicing with a negative index raises AssertionError ('Negative indexing is not supported'), directly contradicting the comment claiming 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically'. A superuser or global-access member sending cursor=0:-5:0 with optimized_pagination=true triggers the negative-offset branch and receives a 500 on every invocation; the comment-asserted safety property is false, so the entire 'advanced feature' is a guaranteed error path rather than a bounded one.

[ADVISORY] New admin-gated behavior is enabled by a raw, unvalidated query parameter (optimized_pagination == 'true') with no feature flag or options entry, and the safety of the negative-offset mode rests entirely on the comment-only invariant that 'permissions are checked at the queryset level' in a generic, reusable paginator class. Once any client or admin UI adopts the parameter, the behavior cannot be centrally disabled or rate-limited without a code deploy; and because OptimizedCursorPaginator performs no scoping itself, any future caller that passes a queryset not pre-filtered by org/tenant silently gets arbitrary-position reads across whatever rows the queryset reaches — the paginator layer provides no guardrail, only an assumption documented in a comment.

[ADVISORY] zpopmin silently evicts up to span_count - 1000 lowest-score (oldest) members from set_key with no metric, log line, or dead-letter path, permanently discarding spans that were accepted into the pipeline but not yet flushed. Under an ingest burst or flusher lag, customers silently lose spans (gaps in traces) while the ingestion path reports success; operators cannot detect, alert on, or tune the eviction because the diff removes the segment_span_count_exceeded metric in buffer.py and adds no replacement telemetry for Lua-side evictions.

[ADVISORY] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result is a ~45-line copy of the existing cursor-pagination get_result logic, already drifted from its source: the base path clamps negative forward offsets (max(0, offset)) while this copy deliberately re-opens the unclamped hole, and the is_prev trimming condition uses the raw offset in both copies. The next pagination boundary fix must be applied in two places; a fix landed in one copy silently misses the other, and the two implementations will keep diverging precisely in the edge-case handling (negative offsets, is_prev trimming) where pagination bugs live.

[BUG] The new `enable_advanced_features and cursor.offset < 0` branch has zero test coverage and is broken on its first execution: it slices `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative start_offset, which raises Django's AssertionError ('Negative indexing is not supported') rather than paginating, so every admin request with a negative-offset cursor under optimized_pagination returns a 500. Any superuser/global-access user sending optimized_pagination=true with a cursor whose offset is negative (Cursor.from_string parses '-5' via int() without restriction) triggers a 500 from the audit-logs endpoint; the comment's claim that 'the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is false, and a single test driving this branch would have caught it. Checked the diff's test files (tests/sentry/spans/consumers/process/test_consumer.py, tests/sentry/spans/consumers/process/test_flusher.py, tests/sentry/spans/test_buffer.py) — none reference OptimizedCursorPaginator, and no paginator or audit-log spec appears in this diff.

[ADVISORY] Every test update mechanically threads a constant `end_timestamp_precise=1700000000.0` through the existing fixtures, so the suite exercises zadd/zscan with all-equal scores and never asserts the new sorted-set semantics: score-based ordering, score round-trip through zscan, or the >1000-span eviction (zpopmin) added in add-buffer.lua. The existing buffer tests do drive the lua script via the redis-backed buffer fixture, but no test creates more than 1000 spans, so a regression in the eviction branch (popping freshly written spans instead of the oldest, or an off-by-one in `span_count - 1000`) passes CI; likewise a regression that corrupts score ordering passes because the flushed-payload assertions are order-insensitive under equal scores. The tests now verify membership of a zset while asserting nothing about the property (score) that motivated the migration.

[ADVISORY] The new dual-branch pagination path (optimized vs. legacy, gated on the raw `optimized_pagination` query param plus superuser/global-access checks) ships with no test in this diff asserting which paginator is selected under each combination of param and privilege level. A regression that flips the gating (e.g., serving the optimized paginator to non-privileged users, or silently ignoring the param) passes the suite; the authorization-coupled branch selection is exactly the kind of logic that needs a truth-table test and none exists — checked the diff's test files and no spec touching organization_auditlogs or this endpoint's get() was modified.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The 'advanced feature' negative-offset branch slices the queryset with a negative start (`queryset[start_offset:stop]` where `start_offset = cursor.offset < 0`), but Django QuerySets raise `ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported.` for negative slice starts — the inline claim that 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is false. Any admin request to the audit-logs endpoint with `optimized_pagination=true` and a negative cursor offset raises ValueError mid-request and returns a 500; the headline feature of the new paginator cannot execute its distinguishing code path at all.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The endpoint switches to OptimizedCursorPaginator with `order_by="-datetime"` but never passes a `key`, while DateTimePaginator (the previous class) sets `key="datetime"` in its own __init__ — so cursor boundary values are computed from the default pk attribute via `math.ceil(value)` while rows are ordered by datetime. Cursor continuation filters on pk values that contradict the -datetime sort order, so page boundaries are wrong: admins browsing audit logs with the optimized flag get skipped and duplicated entries across pages, silently corrupting audit review.

adjudication.rationale: In `organization_auditlogs.py`, the new optimized path switches `paginator_cls` to `OptimizedCursorPaginator` while keeping `order_by="-datetime"`, but does not pass any `key`. In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key`, cursor values are derived from `getattr(item, self.key)` and coerced via `math.floor/ceil`, meaning pagination boundaries depend on whatever default `self.key` `BasePaginator` provides (commonly a PK/id) rather than the `datetime` ordering field. That creates an order/key mismatch: cursors/filters advance by one field while results are sorted by another, which can lead to skipped/duplicated rows across pages for the optimized/admin flow.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The parent-chain redirect limit was silently reduced from 10000 to 1000 and the comment documenting the accepted tradeoff ('theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly') was deleted rather than re-justified. Trace trees whose parent-chain depth is between 1001 and 10000 — which previously resolved to the correct root and were joined correctly — now exhaust the loop and attach spans to a mid-chain ancestor set, producing incorrectly assembled segments; the original accepted constraint was changed with no explicit human acceptance or replacement mitigation.

adjudication.rationale: In `src/sentry/scripts/spans/add-buffer.lua`, the redirect traversal loop was changed from `for i = 0, 10000 do` (with an explicit comment about the 10k-depth tradeoff) to `for i = 0, 1000 do` and the comment was removed. The loop breaks only when `hget` returns nil or the same id; otherwise it continues updating `set_span_id`. If a redirect chain exceeds 1000 links, the loop will terminate due to the iteration cap, leaving `set_span_id` at a non-root mid-chain value and then proceeding to merge spans into that set (`hset` + subsequent union into `set_key`), which can cause incorrect segment assembly for depths 1001–10000 that previously would have resolved under the 10k cap.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new eviction path (`zpopmin` when `span_count > 1000`) silently drops the oldest spans with no metric or log, replacing the previous oversized-segment handling that emitted `metrics.incr(...segment_span_count_exceeded)` and an error log before skipping. Span data loss (previously at least observable and alertable) becomes completely silent: when a segment set exceeds 1000 members the oldest spans are evicted before flush and no operator signal fires, so trace incompleteness is discovered only by users.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds an explicit eviction path in `add-buffer.lua`: when `span_count > 1000`, it does `zpopmin(set_key, span_count - 1000)` with no accompanying metric/log. In parallel, the prior oversized-segment observability in `SpansBuffer._load_segment_data` (the `max_segment_spans` check that emitted `metrics.incr("...segment_span_count_exceeded")` and `logger.error(...)`) is removed when switching from `sscan`/sets to `zscan`/sorted sets. This is a concrete observability regression tied to new behavior (partial eviction instead of skipping), but whether truncation is a “bug” vs intended tradeoff isn’t provable from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The `max_segment_spans` enforcement block was deleted, leaving that setting unenforced on the read side while the write side now uses a hardcoded 1000 cap inside the Lua script — two different, hand-maintained constants where one config used to be the single source of truth. Operators who tune `max_segment_spans` get no effect on actual behavior, and anyone reasoning about the eviction cap must know to look for a magic number buried in a Lua script; the next change to span-count limits gets harder and is likely to miss one of the two sites.

adjudication.rationale: The diff removes the `max_segment_spans` enforcement on the read/load path in `SpansBuffer._load_segment_data` (the block that checked `len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans` and skipped the segment was deleted). Meanwhile, the write/merge path now enforces a hardcoded cap of `1000` spans in `add-buffer.lua` (`if span_count > 1000 then ... zpopmin ...`). This creates a verifiable mismatch: operators tuning `self.max_segment_spans` no longer affect behavior (at least on the read side), and the actual cap is now a magic number in Lua rather than the Python setting.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] BasePaginator.get_result — the shared paginator used by every cursor-paginated endpoint in the codebase — was modified (negative non-prev offsets now clamp to 0 instead of raising ValueError from Django slicing) purely to accommodate the unrelated OptimizedCursorPaginator feature. All existing endpoints silently change behavior for malformed/negative cursor offsets (500 → silent first page) without any of their owners being asked; a shared-class contract was altered as a hidden dependency of the bundled pagination feature rather than as an accepted change.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does change shared pagination behavior in `BasePaginator.get_result`: it now clamps `start_offset = max(0, offset)` for non-`is_prev` cursors, whereas previously `queryset[offset:stop]` would hit Django’s negative-slice error path for negative offsets. This affects every endpoint using `BasePaginator.get_result` (not just the newly added `OptimizedCursorPaginator`), turning a malformed negative offset into a silent “first page” behavior. While not necessarily a correctness defect by itself, it is a concrete, diff-grounded contract/scope change to shared infrastructure that should be explicitly owned/approved rather than bundled as a side effect of the new paginator feature.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result is a ~70-line verbatim copy of BasePaginator.get_result with only the negative-offset branch added, and the copy has already drifted: the is_prev trim compares `len(results) == offset + limit + extra` using the raw offset while the slice above uses `start_offset`. adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result` that reimplements a full cursor pagination flow (cursor init, hits counting, `extra` handling, slicing, is_prev trimming/reversal, `build_cursor`, post_query_filter) rather than composing/reusing existing paginator logic, which is a concrete maintainability/architecture concern introduced by this change. adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] New admin-only pagination behavior is gated on a raw undocumented query parameter (`optimized_pagination == "true"`) with no feature flag or options entry. adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new runtime behavior switch on `request.GET.get("optimized_pagination") == "true"` in `organization_auditlogs.py`, and routes to the new `OptimizedCursorPaginator` when `enable_advanced` is true (superuser or `has_global_access`). adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Replacing `sunionstore` with `zunionstore` changes duplicate-member semantics: zunionstore's default AGGREGATE is SUM, so a payload present in both `set_key` and `span_key`/`parent_key` gets its end_timestamp_precise score doubled instead of deduplicated as under sadd. Re-merged spans get inflated scores (e.g., ~2x epoch seconds, a timestamp far in the future), so the zpopmin eviction orders them as newest and never evicts them while correctly-scored spans get evicted around them — eviction targets the wrong members whenever the merged sets overlap.

adjudication.rationale: In `add-buffer.lua`, `sunionstore` is replaced with `zunionstore` via `redis.call("zunionstore", set_key, 2, set_key, span_key)` and similarly for `parent_key`. No `AGGREGATE` option is provided, so Redis defaults to `SUM` when the same member exists in both input zsets. Since members are `span.payload` and scores are `end_timestamp_precise` (set by `zadd` in `spans/buffer.py`), overlaps will produce doubled (or otherwise summed) timestamp scores. The subsequent eviction logic uses `zpopmin` based on these scores, so inflated scores will change ordering/eviction behavior compared to prior set semantics (dedupe without score mutation), causing incorrect retention/eviction when merged sets overlap.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator is incompatible with the datetime ordering the audit endpoint uses: get_item_key calls math.floor/math.ceil on getattr(item, self.key) where self.key is 'datetime' (order_by='-datetime'), and build_queryset (line 856) filters the DateTimeField against the integer cursor value, so both raise (TypeError on floor(datetime) / ValidationError on datetime__lt 0) on the very first request. adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The 'advanced' negative-offset branch slices the Django queryset with a negative start (queryset[start_offset:stop] with start_offset = cursor.offset < 0), which Django QuerySet does not support — slicing with a negative index raises AssertionError ('Negative indexing is not supported'), directly contradicting the comment claiming 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically'. A superuser or global-access member sending cursor=0:-5:0 with optimized_pagination=true triggers the negative-offset branch and receives a 500 on every invocation; the comment-asserted safety property is false, so the entire 'advanced feature' is a guaranteed error path rather than a bounded one.

adjudication.rationale: In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, when `enable_advanced_features` is true and `cursor.offset < 0`, it sets `start_offset = cursor.offset` (negative) and then does `queryset[start_offset:stop]`. Django `QuerySet` slicing does not support negative indices and raises an `AssertionError` for negative start/stop, so this branch is a guaranteed 500 error path if a client provides a negative offset (the diff even adds comments claiming negative slicing is handled). This defect is directly introduced by the new negative-offset branch and is diff-grounded.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] New admin-gated behavior is enabled by a raw, unvalidated query parameter (optimized_pagination == 'true') with no feature flag or options entry, and the safety of the negative-offset mode rests entirely on the comment-only invariant that 'permissions are checked at the queryset level' in a generic, reusable paginator class. Once any client or admin UI adopts the parameter, the behavior cannot be centrally disabled or rate-limited without a code deploy; and because OptimizedCursorPaginator performs no scoping itself, any future caller that passes a queryset not pre-filtered by org/tenant silently gets arbitrary-position reads across whatever rows the queryset reaches — the paginator layer provides no guardrail, only an assumption documented in a comment.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new behavior toggle in `organization_auditlogs.py` driven directly by `request.GET.get("optimized_pagination") == "true"`, with no feature-flag/config indirection shown, and it is gated only by an admin-ish check (`request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access`). The new `OptimizedCursorPaginator` is a generic reusable paginator that does not apply any org/tenant scoping itself; it operates purely on the provided `queryset` and relies on comments like “permissions are checked at the queryset level” for safety. Those are real, diff-grounded maintainability/guardrail concerns rather than a strictly provable defect in this PR alone (since the auditlogs queryset here is presumably scoped elsewhere).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] zpopmin silently evicts up to span_count - 1000 lowest-score (oldest) members from set_key with no metric, log line, or dead-letter path, permanently discarding spans that were accepted into the pipeline but not yet flushed. Under an ingest burst or flusher lag, customers silently lose spans (gaps in traces) while the ingestion path reports success; operators cannot detect, alert on, or tune the eviction because the diff removes the segment_span_count_exceeded metric in buffer.py and adds no replacement telemetry for Lua-side evictions.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a hard cap in `add-buffer.lua` that silently discards spans: after merging zsets it computes `span_count` and if `span_count > 1000` it calls `redis.call("zpopmin", set_key, span_count - 1000)`, permanently removing the lowest-score members with no metric/log/dead-letter. At the same time, `buffer.py` removes the prior span-count overflow telemetry/guard (`segment_span_count_exceeded` metric + error log + skip logic) in `_load_segment_data`, and no replacement telemetry is added for Lua-side evictions. This introduces undetectable data loss (accepted spans can be dropped before flush) under burst/lag conditions.

The next pagination boundary fix must be applied in two places; a fix landed in one copy silently misses the other, and the two implementations will keep diverging precisely in the edge-case handling (negative offsets, is_prev trimming) where pagination bugs live.

It has already diverged from the modified existing path: the existing paginator now clamps forward offsets via `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`, while `OptimizedCursorPaginator` conditionally re-allows negative offsets when `enable_advanced_features` is set (`start_offset = cursor.offset` if `< 0`). adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The new `enable_advanced_features and cursor.offset < 0` branch has zero test coverage and is broken on its first execution: it slices `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative start_offset, which raises Django's AssertionError ('Negative indexing is not supported') rather than paginating, so every admin request with a negative-offset cursor under optimized_pagination returns a 500. In `organization_auditlogs.py`, this paginator is enabled for superusers/global-access users when `optimized_pagination=true` and passes `enable_advanced_features=True`, making the negative-offset path reachable. adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Every test update mechanically threads a constant `end_timestamp_precise=1700000000.0` through the existing fixtures, so the suite exercises zadd/zscan with all-equal scores and never asserts the new sorted-set semantics: score-based ordering, score round-trip through zscan, or the >1000-span eviction (zpopmin) added in add-buffer.lua. The existing buffer tests do drive the lua script via the redis-backed buffer fixture, but no test creates more than 1000 spans, so a regression in the eviction branch (popping freshly written spans instead of the oldest, or an off-by-one in `span_count - 1000`) passes CI; likewise a regression that corrupts score ordering passes because the flushed-payload assertions are order-insensitive under equal scores. In the tests shown, every added `end_timestamp_precise` is the same constant `1700000000.0` (or `now`), and there is no test change creating >1000 spans. From the diff alone, it’s accurate that the suite updates fixtures mechanically without asserting any score-dependent behavior (ordering/eviction), so regressions in those new branches could plausibly pass.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The buffer key format switches from Redis set to sorted set in the same script (zcard/zunionstore/zpopmin replacing scard/sunionstore), so during a rolling deploy old workers running the previous script (scard/sadd/sunionstore) execute against keys that new workers have already converted to zsets, and Redis raises WRONGTYPE, aborting the whole Lua script. Span ingestion errors for every project whose trace has at least one key created by the other code version during the deploy window; old-code pods and new-code pods crash/fail each other's writes bidirectionally (SADD on a zset and ZADD/ZCARD on a set both raise WRONGTYPE) until all workers are rolled and every pre-existing set-format key expires via set_timeout.

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes the Redis data type for `span-buf:s:{...}:<id>` keys from Set operations (`sadd`, `scard`, `sunionstore`, `sscan`) to Sorted Set operations (`zadd`, `zcard`, `zunionstore`, `zscan`, `zpopmin`) across `add-buffer.lua` and `spans/buffer.py`. There is no compatibility logic to handle pre-existing set-typed keys or mixed-version writers. As a result, during a rolling deploy (or simply with existing keys from the prior version), the new code will run `zcard/zunionstore/zscan` against keys that may still be Sets, and old code would run `sadd/scard/sscan` against keys that may now be ZSETs—both cases produce Redis `WRONGTYPE` and will abort the Lua script / fail ingestion until those keys expire.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] process_spans now writes via p.zadd to set_key while pre-deploy workers still write the same key via p.sadd, so the two writer populations collide on one Redis key with incompatible types. During the rolling deploy of the process consumer, whichever version created the key first wins the type; the other version's p.execute() raises WRONGTYPE (or the Lua script aborts) and the batch of spans in that write is dropped, losing live telemetry for the duration of the rollout.

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes the Redis data structure at `set_key = f"span-buf:s:{{{project_and_trace}}}:{parent_span_id}"` from a Set to a Sorted Set: `process_spans` now writes with `p.zadd(...)` (was `p.sadd(...)`), and the Lua script switches reads/merges from `scard`/`sunionstore` to `zcard`/`zunionstore`. The key name/prefix (`span-buf:s:{...}:...`) is unchanged, and there is no versioning/migration/dual-write logic. In a mixed-version deployment, one version will create the key as SET and the other will treat it as ZSET, causing Redis `WRONGTYPE` errors and dropped writes/script failures as the finding describes.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] _load_segment_data switches sscan to zscan with no migration or dual-read step, so buffered spans stored under the old set format cannot be read by the new flusher — zscan on a set-typed key raises WRONGTYPE. At deploy time, all span data already sitting in the Redis buffer (every set key not yet flushed) becomes unfetchable: the flush pipeline errors, those spans are never written to the event stream, and they silently expire via set_timeout — a permanent loss of all in-flight buffered spans with no error surfaced to users.

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes the Redis data type for span buffer keys `span-buf:s:{...}:<id>` from a Set to a Sorted Set: `process_spans` switches `p.sadd(...)` to `p.zadd(...)` in `src/sentry/spans/buffer.py`, and `_load_segment_data` switches `p.sscan(...)` to `p.zscan(...)`. During a rolling deploy, any in-flight buffered spans already stored as Sets will be read with `ZSCAN`, which in Redis raises WRONGTYPE on set-typed keys, breaking flushing and risking loss when keys expire. The finding is directly supported by the diff’s storage/read changes and lack of migration/dual-read logic.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The consumer now requires val["end_timestamp_precise"] (KeyError if absent), but no producer change in this diff adds the field, so messages already in the spans topic produced before this release — and any produced by not-yet-updated ingest pods during the rolling deploy — crash process_batch. adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The max_segment_spans abort guard (metric, log, del payloads/cursors) is deleted from _load_segment_data and its safety is now delegated solely to the hard-coded 1000-member eviction cap in the Lua script, which is not configurable and does not protect sets that were populated before this deploy. After the change, `_load_segment_data` only enforces `self.max_segment_bytes` while accumulating payloads (`sizes[key] += ...`), so a segment with many small spans can now be fully loaded without any server-side span-count bound. The diff adds a hard-coded `> 1000` eviction in `add-buffer.lua`, but that cap is not configurable (doesn’t reference `max_segment_spans`) and is not enforced in the Python write path shown (`process_spans` now does `p.zadd(...)` without any trimming), so the removed guard is a real regression in protection against oversized segment loads.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator subclasses BasePaginator but calls self.build_queryset() (and self.count_hits/_is_asc), methods that exist only on CursorPaginator/Paginator, so the first request using it raises AttributeError: 'OptimizedCursorPaginator' object has no attribute 'build_queryset'. adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The negative-offset branch slices queryset[start_offset:stop] with a negative start, which Django's QuerySet.__getitem__ rejects with ValueError('Negative indexing is not supported.'), contradicting the inline comment claiming the ORM 'handles negative slicing automatically'. adjudication.rationale: In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, when `enable_advanced_features` is true and `cursor.offset < 0`, it sets `start_offset = cursor.offset` and slices `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative start. The diff also explicitly allows negative offsets in `Cursor.__init__` (now just `self.offset = int(offset)` with a comment). Django `QuerySet.__getitem__` does not support negative slicing/indices and raises `ValueError('Negative indexing is not supported.')`, so a crafted/corrupted cursor containing a negative offset can trigger an exception and likely a 500. This contradicts the inline comment claiming negative slicing is handled automatically.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The zpopmin trim silently deletes the oldest spans (span_count - 1000 lowest end_timestamp scores) with no metric, log, or error result, and the corresponding Python-side guard (metrics.incr('spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded') + logger.error) is deleted from _load_segment_data in the same diff. Once a segment set exceeds 1000 entries, every subsequent insert permanently discards spans, and the flusher then emits segments that are silently missing those spans — incomplete trace data reported as a successful flush with zero operator signal; the pre-existing detection path that logged and counted this condition is removed, so the data loss is invisible to operators and on-call.

adjudication.rationale: In `add-buffer.lua`, when a segment set exceeds 1000 entries the code unconditionally trims with `zpopmin(set_key, span_count - 1000)`, permanently deleting the lowest-score (oldest `end_timestamp_precise`) span payloads without any metric/log/error. In the same diff, `_load_segment_data` in `spans/buffer.py` removes the prior detection/alerting path that enforced `max_segment_spans` (`metrics.incr("spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded")` + `logger.error(...)` and skipping the segment). The new behavior can therefore produce flushed segments missing spans while reporting no operator signal, which is a correctness/data-loss regression visible from the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The max_segment_spans count guard (metric, logger.error, and segment-skip on count overflow) is deleted with no replacement, leaving only the byte-size cap. Sets that exceed the 1000-entry Lua cap (e.g., sets persisted by the pre-deploy sadd implementation that have not yet been touched by the new script, or sets written during a rolling deploy mixing old sadd writers with the new zadd script) are now buffered with unbounded span counts into payloads[key] until the byte cap trips, and the segment_span_count_exceeded metric that previously surfaced this condition no longer exists, so the transition-period anomaly is undetectable.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does remove the `max_segment_spans` overflow guard in `SpansBuffer._load_segment_data` (the block that emitted `segment_span_count_exceeded`, logged an error, and skipped the segment when `len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans`) and does not add an equivalent check in Python. The only remaining in-code protection shown is the byte-size cap (`sizes[key] > self.max_segment_bytes`). While `add-buffer.lua` now caps a ZSET to 1000 entries via `zpopmin`, that cap is not applied to the Python-side `zadd` writer in `process_spans`, and the PR does not show guarantees that all segment keys will be trimmed before loading. However, the finding’s rolling-deploy/old-SET-type scenario and “undetectable transition anomaly” aspects are speculative beyond what the diff alone proves.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] process_batch indexes val["end_timestamp_precise"] directly (unlike the sibling fields, which use val.get), so any Kafka message produced without this field raises KeyError inside the arroyo processing strategy. During a rolling deploy where producers (or backlogged messages in the ingest-spans topic) predate the field, every batch containing such a message raises KeyError and the consumer repeatedly fails the same offset — a poison-message stall on the spans processing pipeline rather than a skip-and-continue.

adjudication.rationale: In `src/sentry/spans/consumers/process/factory.py`, `process_batch` now constructs `Span(..., end_timestamp_precise=val["end_timestamp_precise"], ...)` after `val = cast(SpanEvent, rapidjson.loads(payload.value))`. Unlike `parent_span_id=val.get("parent_span_id")` and the `is_segment_span` logic using `val.get(...)`, this direct dict indexing will raise `KeyError` for any message missing `end_timestamp_precise`. The diff provides no fallback/default handling, so older/backlogged Kafka messages without this field would crash the consumer while processing a batch containing them.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] New behavior is gated on the raw query parameter optimized_pagination (plus an inline is_superuser/has_global_access check) with no feature flag or options entry, and the enable_advanced_features=True flag it feeds only activates the crashing negative-offset branch. If the optimized path misbehaves in production it cannot be disabled without a code deploy (no flag to flip), and the admin-only gate means the failing 500 responses surface only for superusers/global-access members hitting the endpoint with the new parameter, concentrating breakage on the highest-privilege users.

adjudication.rationale: The optimized path is enabled solely via `request.GET.get("optimized_pagination") == "true"` plus an inline privilege check, with no feature flag/config hook shown in the diff (so rollback is only by deploy or by ensuring clients stop sending the param). More importantly, `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result` explicitly allows negative offsets when `enable_advanced_features` is true (`start_offset = cursor.offset` when `< 0`) and then slices the Django queryset with `queryset[start_offset:stop]`. Django QuerySet slicing does not support negative indices and will raise at runtime, producing 500s for requests that carry a cursor with a negative offset (which is now explicitly "allowed" per the new comment in `Cursor`).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The base Paginator clamp handles negative offsets inconsistently: non-prev cursors are silently clamped to page 0 via max(0, offset), while is_prev cursors still pass the negative offset into queryset[start_offset:stop], which Django rejects with ValueError. A client-supplied cursor with a negative offset now silently returns the first page (valid 200 with wrong data) on forward pagination but a 500 on the identical cursor with is_prev set — the same malformed input yields two different failure shapes depending on the is_prev bit, and the wrong-page case gives no error a client could detect.

adjudication.rationale: In `src/sentry/api/paginator.py` the slice start is now clamped only when `not cursor.is_prev` (`start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`). This means a client-provided negative `cursor.offset` will be silently coerced to `0` for forward pagination (returning the first page with no error), but for `is_prev` it will pass the negative offset directly into `queryset[start_offset:stop]`, which Django QuerySet slicing rejects (raising and likely producing a 500). The diff therefore introduces inconsistent handling and the “wrong page with 200” case described is directly implied by the new clamping logic.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The redirect-chain walk cap is reduced from 10000 to 1000 iterations while the code still commits hset(main_redirect_key, span_id, set_span_id) unconditionally after the loop, so chains deeper than 1001 hops store an intermediate node as the resolved segment. Traces whose parent-redirect chains exceed 1000 levels (previously correct up to 10k) now attach spans to an intermediate segment instead of the root, silently mis-associating spans in flushed data with no log or metric — the removed comment explicitly documented this exact failure mode at the old bound.

adjudication.rationale: In `src/sentry/scripts/spans/add-buffer.lua`, the redirect-chain traversal loop cap is reduced from `0, 10000` to `0, 1000`. The loop updates `set_span_id` as it follows redirects, but if the chain is longer than the cap, the loop terminates without reaching a terminal node and the code still unconditionally executes `redis.call("hset", main_redirect_key, span_id, set_span_id)` afterward. This means spans in very deep redirect chains can be permanently redirected to an intermediate `set_span_id` rather than the final/root segment, with no error/metric emitted. The old comment explicitly acknowledged this failure mode at the previous bound, and the new bound increases the likelihood.
